analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal public developer to buy distressed properties and build permanently affordable social housing.
analysis.headline: The Homes Act of 2024 was introduced in the Senate in September 2024 with two Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an independent Housing Development Authority inside HUD with permanent federal backing to buy foreclosed, blighted, and federally assisted rental properties and convert them into "social housing": housing owned by the public or by nonprofits and tenant groups, with permanent affordability rules that bar resale to for-profit investors. At least 40% of units would be set aside for extremely low-income families, rents would be capped at 25% of household income with small annual increases, tenants would get just-cause eviction protections, and residents would sit on the Authority's governing board. It would also repeal the Faircloth Amendment, the 1998 law that froze construction of new public housing units.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who cannot afford market rents, especially extremely low-income families, homeless people, and residents of distressed buildings, would gain access to permanently affordable units shielded from speculation. Existing tenants of covered buildings would get first chance to buy their buildings and just-cause eviction protections. Construction workers would benefit from prevailing-wage and project-labor requirements, and rural and Native communities would get a guaranteed service obligation.

how_it_helps.text: The Authority would acquire distressed, blighted, and federally assisted properties and hold them in perpetuity, conveying them only to nonprofits, tenant organizations, community land trusts, public housing agencies, and governments, with deed restrictions barring resale into the private market [S2].
At least 40% of units in new or rehabilitated social housing would be set aside for extremely low-income families, and at least 70% for low- and extremely low-income families [S2].

Rents in social housing would be set at 25% of household adjusted gross income, with annual increases capped at the lesser of 3% or inflation, and tenants overcharged or wrongfully evicted could sue for damages [S2].

Owners of covered multifamily rental properties would have to give tenants and the Authority 90 days' notice before selling, plus a 30-day first-look period in which tenant organizations and nonprofits get the first opportunity to purchase [S2].

Construction would carry prevailing-wage requirements, project labor agreements on large projects, Buy America sourcing, and a rule that most workers be treated as employees rather than independent contractors [S2].
The bill would repeal the Faircloth Amendment, the 1998 restriction that blocks federal funding for new public housing units [S2].

The Authority's 15-member board would include six residents of public or social housing, and the Authority could use eminent domain and receivership to preserve and create social housing, with limits barring displacement and discriminatory targeting [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the Authority's operations, a public housing repair backlog, and any defaults on the federal government's guaranteed bonds, since the bill authorizes appropriations and sets a maximum contingent liability for its debt. Owners of multifamily rental properties would bear costs from the mandatory sale-notice periods, tenant and nonprofit purchase rights, and first-refusal pricing tied to outstanding debt rather than market value.

drawbacks.text: The program would be expensive and open-ended: the bill authorizes appropriations for the Authority and a public housing backlog and permits the Authority to issue bonds guaranteed by the United States, putting taxpayers on the hook if projects underperform [S2].

The Authority could use eminent domain and would get rights of first refusal and refusal on federally assisted properties at a price limited to outstanding debt plus taxes, which raises good-faith concerns about owners receiving less than market value and about the scale of government acquisition of private property [S2].

Rent caps and profit limits (2% per year on limited equity) could discourage some private capital from maintaining and improving rental properties outside the program, and building a large public portfolio takes years, so relief for renters would be slow to arrive [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real and worsening problem—housing costs that consume a large share of low- and moderate-income budgets—with a structure designed to keep units affordable permanently rather than through subsidies that flow through private owners. The trade-offs are significant: substantial federal spending and contingent liabilities, a large new government real-estate operation with eminent domain powers, and pricing rules that shift value from property owners to tenants and taxpayers. Whether it is good design depends on how well the Authority executed; the bill died before any of that could be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2024 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, and Congress ended without any hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the Homes Act of 2024 on September 18, 2024, joined by Sens. Peter Welch and Jeff Merkley, both Democrats [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on September 18, 2024 [S4].
No further action appears in the bill's history—no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote—before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and investors in multifamily rental properties, who would have faced mandatory sale-notice periods, tenant and nonprofit purchase rights, and debt-based pricing, are better off because the bill never advanced. Tenant groups and nonprofit developers gained nothing from its failure.

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Homes Act of 2024 in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Peter Welch and Jeff Merkley
for.role: Cosponsors, U.S. Senators from Vermont and Oregon
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican senator signed on.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-OH) in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill or reported it out, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored it; it never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.industry: Multifamily rental property owners and investor landlords
industries.note: The bill would require owners of covered multifamily properties to give tenants and the Authority notice before selling, grant tenant organizations and nonprofits the first chance to buy, and allow the Authority to acquire federally assisted properties at a price capped at outstanding debt plus taxes. Housing owned under the program could never be resold into the private market, permanently removing units from speculative investment [S2].

A large new publicly financed construction and rehabilitation pipeline would create work, with prevailing-wage requirements, project labor agreements on large jobs, and local-hire and pre-apprenticeship provisions benefiting workers [S2].

The Authority could buy distressed and nonperforming mortgages and seek to recoup losses from parties that caused distress through fraud, abusive terms, or equity stripping, reducing returns for holders of those assets [S2].

industries.industry: Nonprofit housing providers, community land trusts, and tenant organizations
industries.note: These entities would become the permanent conveyees and operators of the Authority's housing stock, with financing and technical assistance from the Authority, entrenching nonprofit and community ownership as the channel for this public housing supply [S2].
